articles.title: DMARC fails even though SPF and DKIM pass: how alignment actually works
articles.excerpt: You open the headers of a rejected or quarantined message and see something like this: spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=bounce.vendor.com dkim=pass header.d=vendor.com dmarc=fail (p=quarantine) header.from=your…
articles.body: You open the headers of a rejected or quarantined message and see something like this: spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=bounce.vendor.com dkim=pass header.d=vendor.com dmarc=fail (p=quarantine) header.from=yourdomain.com SPF passed. DKIM passed. DMARC failed. That is not a bug, and it is one of the most common DMARC problems after a policy moves off p=none . What DMARC really checks DMARC does not ask "did SPF or DKIM pass?". It asks "did one of them pass for the same domain that appears in the visible From: header ?" That match is called alignment. SPF alignment : the domain in the envelope sender ( smtp.mailfrom / Return-Path) must match the From: domain. DKIM alignment : the d= domain in the DKIM signature must match the From: domain. Only one of the two has to align.

articles.title: Your Polymarket Backtest Is Profitable. Here Are 4 Things to Test Before Going Live
articles.excerpt: A backtest can show positive returns and still tell you very little about how a trading bot will behave in a live market. The problem isn't necessarily the strategy. It may be the assumptions surround…
articles.body: A backtest can show positive returns and still tell you very little about how a trading bot will behave in a live market. The problem isn't necessarily the strategy. It may be the assumptions surrounding it. If a simulation assumes every order fills at the expected price, ignores trading costs, or uses information that would not have been available at decision time, its results can look better than the strategy deserves. Before deploying a Polymarket bot, I would test four things. Does the strategy use only information available at the time? Look-ahead bias occurs when a backtest uses information that would not have been available when the simulated decision was made.
articles.author: Dexoryn

articles.title: Calculate average order value from Shopify orders with the Admin GraphQL API
articles.excerpt: Disclosure: I work on Brix, a Shopify cart app. This post is about the maths and the API, and Brix is mentioned only at the end. Average order value (AOV) is total revenue divided by the number of ord…
articles.body: Disclosure: I work on Brix, a Shopify cart app. This post is about the maths and the API, and Brix is mentioned only at the end. Average order value (AOV) is total revenue divided by the number of orders. The formula is one line. Getting a number you can trust takes a bit more care, because the totals Shopify gives you include things you may not want to count. In this post we will pull orders with the Admin GraphQL API and compute AOV in Node.js, while handling the usual traps: test orders, cancelled orders, refunds, shipping and taxes. What you need A Shopify store, ideally a development store to try this on. A custom app with an Admin API access token and the read_orders scope. By default this covers the last 60 days of orders.

articles.body: My AI coding workflow changes every few months, so I give it version numbers. New tools ship, models get better, and steps that needed hand-holding last spring now run on their own. v1 was plan mode and a hand-written SPEC.md . v2 turned that into TracerKit. This post is v3: every step now lives in helderberto/agent-skills . The idea of v3 fits in one line: each step that used to be a prompt is now a skill, and each "please remember to" is now a check that fails. Why I moved off TracerKit (v2) TracerKit worked, but it was a separate tool with its own release cycle. Every tweak to a step meant a change there, a release, and an update in each project. I wanted a simpler way to ship updates and add new skills. I was already keeping my other skills in agent-skills.

articles.body: When Robert Altman's M*A*S*H arrived in theaters in 1970, its irreverent approach to the Korean War was unlike anything audiences had seen before. articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 23, 2007: NASA launches Harmony module to ISS on STS-120 space shuttle mission
articles.excerpt: On October 23, 2007, the space shuttle Discovery launched the Harmony module to the International Space Station. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 23, 2007, the space shuttle Discovery launched the Harmony module to the International Space Station . The Harmony module is a utility hub 14 feet wide and 24 feet long, or about the length of a minibus. It joins the European Space Agency's Columbus module and Japan's Kibo laboratory and serves as the crew quarters for the American astronauts. Once it was installed, the space station grew from about the size of a three-bedroom house to something more like a five-bedroom house. When astronauts delivered Harmony to the space station , they left it temporarily attached to the Unity node. After the shuttle left, astronauts used the space station's robotic arm to move the shuttle docking port out of the way at the Destiny module.

articles.excerpt: This incredible composite image of Orionid meteors was captured as Earth passed through the debris trail shed by Halley's Comet.
articles.body: Tim McCollum captured a stunning view of Orionid meteors in the early hours of Oct. 21. (Image credit: Tim McCollum) Astrophotographer Tim McCollum captured a spectacular view of Orionid meteors sharing the night sky with a host of deep sky wonders on Oct. 21, as the annual shooting star display ramped up to peak activity. Comet 1P/Halley may be over 3 billion miles (4.8 kilometers) from Earth , but that didn't stop it from putting on a breathtaking display earlier this week, as particles cast off by the ancient wanderer carved a fiery path through the autumn sky. McCollum was able to capture a trio of vivid Orionid meteors as they streaked through the night sky above the city of Toccoa, Georgia, between 3-4 a.m. on Oct. 21.
